2112165116921659588.text:
My biggest takeaways from @AnthropicAI interpretability researcher @mlpowered:

1. Predicting the next token requires understanding the universe. Language models got better than humans at predicting the next token around 2019. Once a model masters the easy tokens (sentence structure, then basic facts), the only ones left are hard, like the final paragraph of a PhD thesis. To finish “The capital of the state that contains Dallas is . . .,” a model has to know that Dallas is in Texas and that Texas’s capital is Austin.

2. LLMs plan ahead, even though they write one token at a time. This was one of Emmanuel’s team’s most surprising findings. When a model writes poetry, it doesn’t stumble into a rhyme. Looking at intermediate thinking states during poetry generation, researchers found that as soon as the model finishes the first line, it has already picked the word that will end the second (“rabbit”), then refers back to that plan for every word after.

3. Anthropomorphizing AI can often be a useful approach when trying to predict how they will behave. Models learn from human text and develop representations of the world from it. Training on millions of dialogues is like training an actor to play every part, and your chats with Claude are literally formatted as a script (“Human: . . . Assistant: . . . ”). In Emmanuel’s words, “Something that’s mimicking a human is really close and is much closer than a program.”

4. Interpretability research looks more like neuroscience than software engineering. The job involves taking a system you did not design and running experiments to infer why it behaves as it does. You examine seemingly meaningless lists of numbers, pass the model huge volumes of text, and watch for patterns that activate from different inputs—not unlike the methods used in brain imaging studies. “A lot of what we do feels so much closer to biology than to engineering."

5. Models can tell you about only a small slice of what they’re thinking. Emmanuel’s team found that just a small subset of a model’s internal representations, which they call the “J space,” can be reported back if you ask the model what it was thinking about. They compare it to a theory of the human mind where most processing happens below the surface. In one experiment, they swapped “Spanish” for “French” inside the J space. Asked what language a passage was in, the model said French. Asked to simply continue the passage, it kept writing Spanish.

6. Studying models closely often raises more questions than it answers. Emmanuel notes that the confident claims that LLMs are “just X” or “nothing more than Y” almost always come from people who haven’t studied their internal workings. His own experience is the inverse: studying the models closely has increased his uncertainty, not reduced it. The complexity that emerges from training is consistently underestimated from the outside. “I find that the more you look inside, the less certain you are about how they work.”

7. Even the people who build AI models don’t fully understand how they work. As Emmanuel describes it, models are grown, not built. “To make them is not to understand them.” Engineers write the code, pour enormous amounts of data through it, and a model’s capabilities emerge. That’s why his team exists. Their job is to open the model up and figure out what it’s actually doing between your prompt and its answer.

8. Interpretability as a field is small, young, and open to newcomers. Emmanuel estimates the field at hundreds of researchers, split between major labs and academic groups. Because it is so new, getting started doesn’t necessarily require deep prior expertise. He points to platforms like Neuronpedia, which hosts models and lets anyone run interpretability experiments directly. “It’s such a new field that the on-ramp is mostly self-studying and reading some of the key papers. There’s so much to explore that if you’re at all curious, you should just give it a try.”

New Princeton Univ +  Google paper finds that the decision model most accurate on isolated questions solved only 69.5% of agent tasks, while a 4B model trained on agent states solved 91.5%.

Agent harnesses call a big LLM at every step, which makes long tasks slow and costly. Yet most of those calls just pick from a list, like which tool to use next.

Their harness asks a fast decision model each multiple-choice question and uses its answer only above a confidence threshold fitted on the agent's own runs. They also trained AgentDecision-4B on states the agent actually reaches, including after its own mistakes.

On tasks like their training data, 4B models trained this way made agents 81.1% to 89.0% cheaper and up to 2.5x faster. Success stayed within 3 points, while handing over every tool choice with no threshold lowered success by 19.0 points.

To hand routine agent choices to a small model, train it and set its confidence threshold on your agent's own runs.

– arxiv. org/abs/2610.21412

Title: "JevAgentHarness: Benchmarking, Deploying and Training Decision Models That Share Control with LLMs"

AI agents that hunt security bugs spend 60.4% of their tokens understanding code and reasoning about how to trigger the bug, so that is where cost cuts should aim.

AI agents hunting security bugs can burn millions of tokens without producing an input that crashes the program. Across 200 runs from 4 agents, 60.4% of tokens went to understanding code and reasoning about how to trigger the bug.

Existing cost-saving methods rarely helped. Only 24.4% of head-to-head comparisons with the plain agent kept success at lower cost.

So they built AVRI, a tool that returns related code together and saves the links between program input and the unsafe operation. On 20 new tasks, it cut total cost by 18.0% for Codex and 23.7% for OpenCode without lowering success or recall.

Before adding generic cost tricks to a security agent, measure where its tokens go and let it reuse what it learned about the code.

I do not know how things are in other countries. But in Denmark, when I follow the coverage of the unrest in France on our two public-service television broadcasters, the explanation I keep hearing is this:

France has spent years cutting back on upper secondary education. Classes are overcrowded. Add teacher shortages and excessive centralisation, and young people take to the streets.

That is only half the truth. And when you peddle half the truth, you are, as we know, also peddling half a lie.

Here is what can be pieced together from the French quality press and the official figures.

France’s public spending per upper-secondary pupil is above the OECD average. That should complicate any account which treats a lack of money as the whole explanation.

There is some truth in the criticism: some lycées have large classes, and the French education system is centralised and bureaucratic.

One example worth mentioning is Parcoursup, the higher education admissions platform. I suspect it would be a strong contender in any international competition for bureaucratic opacity and unnecessary stress.

But, as I have already said, this is only half the truth.

The other half concerns what teachers and school leaders are being asked to endure. 

I admit that this is anecdotal. But recently, a math teacher from Metz described in a long and serious post on X how the teachers simply burn out at the most problematic high schools. We need to dig deeper into this constant attrition of skilled high school teachers.

Why are schools being left to carry so much of the burden?

French politicians are no different from politicians elsewhere in Europe.

They want as many young people as possible to complete upper secondary education and go on to higher education. For the usual reasons: education is supposed to break the cycle of inherited disadvantage, while higher education is supposed to raise productivity. I find those arguments only partly convincing when these benefits are treated as automatic consequences of expanding access.

In my view, France faces a problem we also know in Denmark: schools are being asked to compensate for failures of integration and basic socialisation that extend far beyond the classroom.

The danger is that, instead of institutions civilising their pupils, disruptive pupils end up barbarising the institutions.

No school can function properly if it is expected to tolerate young people who turn up unprepared, have no interest in learning and spend their time causing trouble and destroying the learning environment.

It is hardly surprising that such conditions can wear teachers down. They cannot reasonably be expected to shoulder the entire responsibility for correcting mistakes that the French political elite has spent decades making.

La France Insoumise and other radical organisations have encouraged the protests and blockades. Mélenchon has called for non-violence. However, this formal appeal for moderation appears symbolic when the LFI mayor of Saint-Denis simultaneously allows himself to be photographed among demonstrators and calls their actions justified.

Le Point has meanwhile reported on mobilisation by Étudiants musulmans de France and its cooperation with RED Jeunes. The former is linked to the Muslim Brotherhood milieu in a French Interior Ministry report; the two organisations helped establish the anti-Islamophobia collective Génération EDR, whose links to the antifascist group La Jeune Garde are also described by Le Point.

That is the kind of convergence I mean by Islamogauchism in practice.

The flags also deserve attention. Palestinian, Moroccan and Algerian flags have appeared at some of the protests, including scenes of disorder. To me, this is another indication that, for some participants, the agenda extends beyond class sizes and school budgets.

We do not yet know the full picture. But what concerns me is the apparent convergence, within parts of this movement, of several forms of radicalism: Antifa activism. Decolonial ideology. Islamogauchism. Islamist networks that have learnt from the left to speak fluent woke.

That is why I do not think it entirely misplaced to speak of an “Islamogauchist intifada” when describing this radical current within the French protests.

The wider protest wave has already spread to Belgium and Italy.

The Danish public-service coverage I have seen gives me far too little of this side of the story.

Two questions: Is it the same elsewhere in the Western world? And if so, why?

יש כאן שאלה טובה מאוד שאני רוצה להפוך לציוץ נפרד -

״למה בחלק מהרחובות יש בלגן אטומי וברחובות ליד (שבהן יש חנויות טובות לביזה) אין כלום?״ 

התשובה די פשוטה: הפאטרן הזה של איזורים שבהם יש ביזה נרחבת ואיזורים ממש ליד שאין בהם כלום הוא סימפטום של העובדה שעבודת הונדליזם והביזה היא עבודה מקצועית, מתוכננת ומתוזמרת מראש. 

ואני אסביר: 

מה שמאפיין את כל ההתפרעויות בצרפת עד כה, כמו ניצחון סן ז׳רמן, ״חג המוזיקה״ וכו׳ הוא ה״הרסנות הספונטנית״ שנוצרת על ידי הגעה של המונים של אנשים מהפרוורים הקשים אל תוך הערים הגדולות בעיקר בשעות הערב - בחסות העלטה ובחסות המון גדול שזורם ברחובות - קל מאוד לבצע מעשי ונדליזם ושוד שלמשטרה קשה להבחין בהם עד שכבר ״מאוחר מדי״ או לפחות, זה מאפשר מספיק זמן פעולה קריטי לפני שכוחות משטרה יכולים להגיע למקום. בגלל זה, הצורה של איזורי השוד במקרים האלה תמיד היתה חופפת לצירי ההתקדמות של ההמון. 

אתמול קרה דבר שונה בתכלית. 

היו צירי תנועה של הפגנות שאושרו על ידי רשויות המשטרה, היו מעט התפרעויות שבוצעו גם לאורך צירים אלה אבל אלו היו בעיקר התפרעויות ספונטניות רגילות ולא מאורגנות. 

**רוב הנזק** בוצע באיזורים **רחוקים יחסית** מההפגנות והוא בוצע בצורה מאורגנת בשיטה חכמה מאוד - קודם כל, צוותים מיומנים ערמו בריקדות סביב סקטור מסויים. בריקדות שלא נתקלו בשום התנגדות משטרתית כי פשוט המשטרה לא היתה שם כי היא היתה עסוקה באיבטוח הציר של ההפגנות המורשות. 

אחרי שהבריקדות הוקמו, בדרך כלל הן גם הוצתו. אבל לא רק הבריקדות הוצתו אלא גם הוצתו מספר מוקדים בסמוך כמו מכוניות או חזיתות של בתי עסק, דלתות עץ וכו׳. המטרה היתה שתושבים יתקשרו למכבי האש שישלחו ניידות כיבוי אש שתאלצנה למשוך מים מברזי ההסנקה ולכוון את מאמצי הכיבוי למספר מוקדים [בד״כ בצומת] מה שמייצר דה-פקטו - חסימה יעילה של צירי התנועה - מעבר לבריקדות הבוערות עצמן. 

מהרגע הזה, הבוזזים היו חופשיים בעצם לשבור באין מפריע את חזיתות החנויות שעיניינו אותם. העניין הוא שהם גם ״עמדו בזמנים״ לפי הדיווחים, שעת ה-ש׳ היתה 16:30. -  כשאתה בוזז בתוך סקטור ״מאובטח״ ע״י בריקדות בוערות וניידות כיבוי שמתחילות לזרום *רחוק* מצירי ההפגנות וכשכל הביזה מתרחשת סימולטנית - גם כוח משטרה של מאות אלפי שוטרים - לא יצליח להגיע במהירות (על ידי סיורים רכובים או טרנזטים - כי הצירים סגורים) או לזרום בזמן בריצה לכל אתרי הביזה כדי לעצור אותה. 

זה מה שבעצם מוכיח שמדובר היה בהתארגנות מקצועית עם יד מכוונת וצוותים ממושמעים. על מי נופל החשד? על הצוותים המיומנים של אנטיפה ואירגוני שמאל רדיקליים אחרים, כולל ״מוחים מקצועיים״ שמגיעים מחו״ל. על אנשי ״צרפת הבלתי נכנעת״ של מלנשון ועל סוכנים של רוסיה הפוטינסקית. [זוכרים את מגיני הדוד הכחולים שצוירו על בתים של יהודים מיד אחרי ה-7 בספטמבר? את בית הכנסת שנצבע בירוק? את סימני הידיים האדומות על האנדרטה לזכר השואה? את החבלה במערכות הכוונת הרכבות לפני המשחקים האולימפיים? - כל אלו הוכחו כפעולות חבלה רוסיות].

המודוס אופרנדי הזה הוא גם מה שמסביר את ה״פליאה״ בקרב אנשי בובו [השמאל הבורגני הצרפתי] שמצייצים ציוצים בסגנון ״על איזה מהומות מדברים אני גר פה בפריז והרחוב שלי מלא חנויות ושקט״. כן כפרה. אתה לא באיזור שטורגט מראש על ידי מארגני ה״מחאה״. ולכן ״לא הבחנת בכלום״.

I promised a quick benchmark and here it is

Adding DeepSeek actually wasn't all that effective as you can see I ended up doing some stuff with Keenable 

Threw this into our funding round benchmark next to Google, TinyFish and a newer API called Keenable, running the same 48 queries over Oct 11 to 17 and grading everything until we had 318 real equity rounds, 139 of them Series A, B or C

On its own this only caught 26.1% of the rounds and 41% of the Series A, B and C, while Google caught 68.9% and is still the best single source we tested

Where this shines is what comes back raw, because 56% of its results were a real round with no model cleaning anything, against 26.7% for Google, 22% for TinyFish and 17.3% for Keenable

The big surprise was Keenable, which found 53 rounds no other API had, while Google found 38 on its own, this found 16 and TinyFish 6

So on top of the Google plus TinyFish setup we run today, which caught 71.4%, adding this got us to 78% and adding Keenable instead got us to 89.6%, with all four landing at 94.7%

Keenable's raw results are the noisiest of the four, but once you put a simple headline filter in front of it, 70% of what's left is a real round by the named company, vs 66.7% for this, 57.3% for TinyFish and 48.7% for Google

We also tested turning company names into domains with an exact host match and no model, and Keenable had the right site somewhere in the top 5 for 75% of companies, Google 73.5%, TinyFish 70.5% and this only 45%

Google still puts the right site first most often at 63.5%, so it's the one to use if you only take the top result

If you try this one, its dates are stamped at Beijing midnight, so after:D before:D gets you a true single day and before:D+1 quietly covers two

Also split OR queries into one search per term, because the 50-result cap piles onto one or two terms, which got us 2.4 to 2.7x more unique URLs here, and splitting multi-site OR got Keenable 3.1x

Cost barely matters at this volume, with this at about $0.03 a day, Google $0.007, TinyFish free and Keenable $0.24 at list price or $0 inside its free 100k requests a month

Review: Cyberpunk Edgerunners 2 is a masterful follow-up that easily lives up to the extremely high bar set by Season 1.

Animation is 10/10, the story is amazing, and the new cast perfectly represents what Night City should be. All of it is backed by an incredible soundtrack composed by Tsuneo Imahori.

This is not a rehash of Season 1. Season 2 feels different, yet somehow familiar. It tells a more personal story that deals with themes of revenge, loss, generational trauma, and the heavy toll it can cost you. There are no love stories this time around - just the cold, brutal reality of Night City.

While the narrative takes center stage, there are still plenty of hype moments and big action set pieces. Everything is done with the exact same level of quality as the original, and the pacing is flawless from start to finish.

The new cast perfectly mirrors Cyberpunk 2077's lifepaths:

• D is a Nomad seeking revenge on Arasaka for massacring his clan.

• Talia comes from a Corpo background, carrying the physical and mental weight of a heavily modified body.
 
• Roman & Kingsley are both Street Kids taking on grimy jobs for cash, each representing a different generation.

These characters are not what I expected. The chaos is grounded by Roman, who acts as the observer, documenting everything through an old school video camera. Roman is the sole voice of reason on the show, and his relationship with D serves as the backbone of the season. They become acquainted by pure chance early on - but of course, things quickly start to go left.

The VHS aesthetic plays a huge part in the cinematic direction of the season. Studio Trigger uses VHS filters and scanlines brilliantly, flipping between video recordings and the raw, unfiltered perspective from behind the screen. The entire thing feels much more cinematic, blending 90s anime influences and a variety of different art styles that somehow all still work perfectly together.

Rogue AI and cyberpsychosis hang over the entire season. Edgerunners 2 explores the lasting effects of going psycho, and what happens when a giant megacorp experiments with things they can't control.

Of course, it wouldn't be Edgerunners without some absolutely crushing moments. Plans fall apart, people are betrayed, and there are some genuinely tragic backstories.

Each character deals with their trauma differently - but unlike Season 1, it ends on a slightly more hopeful note that perfectly encapsulates the season's core themes.

For fans of the game, there are PLENTY of references to Cyberpunk 2077. I lost count of the amount of locations and easter eggs I recognized.

There are entire neighborhoods that I vividly remember exploring in-game, and it's all translates beautifully to animation. Edgerunners remains one of the best video game adaptations of all time.

As for connections to Season 1... you'll just have to watch!

Cyberpunk Edgerunners 2 is easily one of the best animated series I've seen since the 2022 original. Studio Trigger delivered yet again with next level production value, soundtrack, and animation.

It expands on Mike Pondsmith's universe beautifully, with zero drop-off in quality, and a new story that enhances the already excellent worldbuilding.

If you're a fan of the game, or the first season, this is an absolute must watch. It explores the effects of body modification, generational trauma, and how a giant megacorp like Arasaka can destroy countless lives.

Better yet, Edgerunners 2 leaves the door wide open for future seasons - and maybe even Cyberpunk 2.

Final Score: 9.5/10

Still tracking to "early 2027":

Bluebirds 14-16 have arrived at Cape Canaveral for launch, while bluebirds 17-50 are in some form of production. Meanwhile, the launch schedule remains more fluid and has generally lagged expectations. At present, ASTS is heavily dependent on SpaceX's Falcon-9 through year end, before Blue Origin's New Glenn 3 is expected to return to the launch pad. ASTS also remains engaged and in qualification with multiple other launch vehicles. Longer term, we believe that launch vehicle diversity is key to sustaining constellation expansion beyond the base 45 satellites required for commercialization. Overall, the ASTS constellation is "when, not if," and we highlight recent performance tests to validate constellation viability. 

Spectrum is nice, partnerships are better:

This provides SPCX with ~80MHz of aggregate spectrum (14MHz, low-band, 65 MHz mid-band). Note: The US is ~6% of global landmass). The bottom line is that Starlink has significantly less capacity (<5% in our estimation) due to frequency reuse to support a large subscriber base for primary services, vs complementary satellite coverage to plug in terrestrial coverage gaps as targeted by ASTS.   

Sovereign constellations and other issues: 
ASTS continues to established itself as a unique and reliable neutral third-party partner for terrestrial MNOs and governmental organizations. Enki impregnates Ninsar, who gives birth to Ninkura under the same bizarre conditions. Another generation follows, with another pregnancy lasting just nine days.

This is a repeated pattern of divine reproduction.

For decades, people reporting alleged encounters with nonhuman intelligence have described some very strange reproductive experiences.

Unexplained pregnancies. Pregnancies that allegedly disappear. Claims of reproductive procedures and children believed to be part human and part something else.

None of those claims has been established as evidence of NHI activity.

Were they simply telling stories about gods whose bodies operated outside human limitations?

That's certainly possible.

But what originally inspired these accounts?

The Sumerians didn't describe nine day pregnancies by accident. They deliberately repeated the same sequence across several generations of divine beings.

I am interested in why reproduction, unusual births, and the creation of new generations appear so often in ancient accounts of divine beings.

Why do some of those same themes continue to appear in modern claims involving nonhuman intelligence?

Were the Sumerians imagining what divine reproduction might look like, or were these stories preserving something they believed they knew about beings different from themselves?

Capital is getting more selective.

And the market is showing what happens when everyone crowds into the same trade.

AI stocks are under pressure. Foreign investors are pulling billions from India. Michael Burry is warning about weakening market breadth.

Meanwhile, tokenized-stock platforms are competing for capital onchain.

These stories share one question:

Where does capital go when yesterday’s winners stop looking so obvious?

Richard Bernstein of Janus Henderson argues that the AI sell-off could eventually benefit small caps by repricing capital and improving access to financing.

A major semiconductor ETF closed nearly 14% below its October high, while chip stocks recorded eight consecutive sessions of declines.

But a correction in crowded trades doesn’t guarantee a rotation into smaller companies. Higher inflation and borrowing costs can hurt them too.

India offers another example.

Foreign investors have sold more than $33B of Indian equities this year, according to the figures in the report.

Yet domestic institutions bought $8.1B in September alone.

Same market. Different positioning.

India’s Finance Minister @nsitharaman adds another dimension: capital outflows and the concentration of investment in AI and the US remain concerns.

Michael Burry’s warning adds a different risk.

An index can keep rising even as fewer stocks do the heavy lifting. His historical analysis highlights how inflation-adjusted returns can remain weak for years after major market peaks.

Now look at tokenized equities.

The October 18 snapshot from Castle Labs and CoinGecko showed:

@bstocksfinance: $1.02B in tokenized asset value, with $380.3M in 24-hour volume.

@xStocksFi: $837.2M in tokenized asset value, with $46.9M in 24-hour volume.

@Ondo: $822.6M in tokenized asset value, with $103.2M in 24-hour volume.

The difference is revealing.

bStocks leads in reported asset value, but each platform shows a different level of trading activity.

Asset value isn’t trading volume. Trading volume isn’t liquidity. Neither alone proves durable demand.

Still, tokenization is creating another competition for capital.

Listing more assets is easy to measure.

Getting investors to hold them, trade them, and access their value efficiently is the harder part.

That’s the connection across these stories.

AI shows the risks of crowded positioning.

India shows the tension between foreign selling and domestic demand.

Burry highlights the fragility that can hide beneath an index rally.

Tokenized equities show the fight to build new destinations for capital.

The next winners won’t necessarily be the assets with the loudest narratives. They’ll be the markets and platforms that give capital a compelling reason to stay.

Capital follows opportunity.

But it stays where access, liquidity, and risk make sense.

themes.summary: Founders are sharing how they built AI agents (Hermes, a citation-and-email finder) that do lead generation and outbound work at a fraction of headcount cost, echoing talk that Salesforce-style SDR roles are being automated away.

themes.name: Scraping any site into an agent skill
themes.summary: A walkthrough shows connecting Apify via MCP to pull data from Maps, Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn and YouTube, then packaging it into a single skill that finds and scores prospects, a template for how marketers are wiring AI into real workflows.
